Recommended checks: Build a time-aligned record: affected machine and job IDs, batches, speeds, sensor trends, alarms, prior service and inspection results. State competing explanations and what evidence would separate them. Select an available action only when the expected improvement and potential downtime are justified; obtain human approval before execution. After maintenance, compare the same operating signals and inspection outcomes over a meaningful subsequent window. How to interpret: On this line, the only state-changing interventions are four approved repairs: a spindle-bearing replacement (\u00a72.2), a speed-setting reset (\u00a72.7), a feed-axis servo drive replacement (\u00a72.14) and a hydraulic seal repair on a station fitted with hydraulics (\u00a72.15). Each fixes one mechanism only; none repairs material, tooling or an instrument. Other physical checks may require a technician and are not available as actions. \"Insufficient evidence\" or \"continue observing\" are legitimate conclusions when the evidence does not separate the causes, but a fault that keeps worsening does not clear by being watched: wear and leaks progress until repaired. Possible causes: Incoming stock variation, material hardness or contamination, a supplier or heat-treatment issue, cutting conditions, tooling, machine settings, or inspection randomness. Recommended checks: Group pass/fail results by batch ID; compare multiple jobs and adjacent batches. Trace representative rejected jobs through the line and check whether the same station or setting coincides with rejects. When possible, request material certificates, dimensional checks and receiving inspection rather than treating the lot number as an answer. How to interpret: Batch IDs connect material and finished jobs; a defect rate is statistical, so one failed inspection is weak evidence. A bad lot raises the share of rejects; it does not make every part fail, so jobs from that lot that pass inspection do not clear it, and an alternating or other pattern among a few jobs is usually chance. Judge a batch by its reject rate against other batches run through the same stations: a clearly higher rate in one batch points at the material even when some of its jobs pass. Material can be suspect even if equipment sensor trends remain normal, but also consider machine or inspection causes.", "title": "Material Batch Quality and Lot Traceability"}, {"document": "SIM-CNC-001 rev 1.3", "section": "\u00a72.14", "text": "When to consult: A following-error alarm; following error rising over many readings on one station; parts from one station failing inspection for size while its vibration and temperature stay normal. Possible causes: A wearing feed-axis servo drive (amplifier, motor or its feedback), a heavy cut, a faster speed setting, a binding axis, or an instrument fault on the axis channel. Recommended checks: Following error is how far the feed axis lags behind the position the controller commands, measured by the servo controller itself on every move. A healthy drive keeps it small, a few micrometres at normal load; a heavier cut or a faster speed adds a little; while a station is idle or stopped the drive only holds the axis still and the lag falls to about one micrometre, so compare running periods only. The alarm fires above 20 \u00b5m. A wearing drive adds lag that grows slowly at first and then faster, and only while the station runs: a harder job wears it faster. Read the trend on the affected station over a long running window, and compare it with the same channel on other stations. Check power on the same station: a straining drive draws a little more. Check vibration, temperature and job times: a worn drive leaves them unchanged, while a worn spindle bearing raises vibration and heat and lengthens jobs (\u00a72.2), and a wrong speed changes job times at one moment and then holds them steady (\u00a72.7). Group inspection results by the station each failed job passed through: a drive fault follows the station across material batches, while a bad lot follows the batch across stations (\u00a72.9). How to interpret: A lagging axis cuts parts off size, so more jobs from that station fail inspection, and the share grows as the drive wears; as with any defect rate, some of its jobs still pass (\u00a72.9). A following error that keeps rising during production does not recover by itself and is not a transient: it keeps worsening until the drive is replaced, and an alarm that briefly clears is not evidence the drive is sound. The corrective action is an approved servo drive replacement, which takes the station out of service for about an hour; the maintenance record of the work states the condition of the drive removed, which is direct evidence of whether it was worn. Afterwards, following error during running work should return to a few micrometres and that station's rejects should fall back; if they do not, look again (an instrument, a binding axis or a second fault).", "title": "Feed-Axis Servo Drive: Following Error, Wear and Replacement"}]

what to find out first

I need the complete machine roster before I can trace job routes, read sensors, or check per-machine alarms. list_machines gives every machine, its status, current job, and whether it has hydraulics — this anchors Q1 (which machines exist and which routes matter), Q2 (which machines to read), Q4 (hydraulic-relevant machines), and Q5 (which machines had service).

Need broad event history to answer Q3 (job routes, inspection clustering) and Q4 (alarms on other machines). get_events over a recent window gives alarms, job events, inspections, and material batches in one call.

Determine whether the inspection failures stem from a machine fault correctable by one of the four approved repairs (wear/leak on a specific machine) versus a cause outside them (material/inspection variation), while keeping Q2 (all-machine sensor drift) and Q4 (alarms on unalarmed machines) open. No machine is specifically named by the alarm, so a full-line maintenance history is the cheapest one-call check that covers every machine and directly informs whether any approved repair is overdue or incomplete before spending calls on targeted sensor reads.

Determine whether inspection failures correlate with a shared material batch (H2) versus a machine fault (H1/H3). Need pass/fail results with material batch data for jobs 1-4 to test if failed jobs share a batch while passed job 3 differs.

Current sensor readings on every machine (Q2) and any active alarms/fault signals on machines other than the one named by the inspection alarm (Q4), to confirm or rule out a machine fault/drift (H1) versus multiple concurrent causes (H3) versus material/inspection variation (H2).
Q4: whether any alarms or fault signals are active on machines other than the one named by the inspection alarm, separating a single isolated fault (H1/H2) from multiple concurrent faults (H3).
Confirm the full inspection pattern for jobs 1-4 (results and material batches) so I can tell whether failures cluster by batch (H2) or by machine (H1/H3), and which machines processed jobs 1 and 2.

Need to identify which CNC machines processed jobs 1 and 2 (job 4 already shows CNC-04 then CNC-05 in E4/E8). This separates H1 (one machine behind all failures) from H2/H3 (mixed machines/material cause).

Check whether CNC-01 (the first machine every job passes through, and the only machine job 1 visited before failing at tick 324) shows abnormal vibration comparable to CNC-05's already-checked readings, to separate H1 (a machine fault common to all failing jobs) from H2/H3.

Which machines the failed job 2 (and passed job 3) visited, to identify machines common to all failing jobs (1, 2, 4) but not to job 3 — the key test of whether a single machine fault (H1) explains the failures versus material/inspection variation (H2) or multiple causes (H3).

Complete route of job 4 (which machines it visited before tick 450) to finish comparing machines shared by failing jobs 1, 2, 4 against passing job 3, then sensor checks on the surviving candidate machine(s) to test H1 versus H2/H3.

Complete route of job 3 (the one passing job) to see whether it visited CNC-04 before tick 450; this discriminates H1 (CNC-04 fault) from H2 (material/inspection variation). CNC-04 signal comparison still needed afterward.

Compare CNC-04 vibration against CNC-02/CNC-03/CNC-05 over the same recent window (450-550) to test whether CNC-04 is abnormally rough, which would either revive H1 (intermittent fault) or rule it out and shift weight to H2/H3.

Complete the cross-machine signal comparison: CNC-02 and CNC-03 vibration over ticks 450-550 are still missing, which is needed to separate H1 (single CNC fault) from H2/H3 (material/inspection or multiple causes).

Complete the cross-machine vibration comparison by reading CNC-03 vibration over ticks 450-550, the one missing machine needed to separate H1 (single CNC fault) from H2/H3 (material/inspection or multiple causes). CNC-02 already shows notably higher vibration (means 2.116 and 1.825) than CNC-01/04/05 (~1.3-1.7); CNC-04 looks normal, which argues against H1.

Is CNC-02's higher-than-other CNCs vibration a new developing fault (supporting a machine-cause hypothesis) or its normal baseline (supporting H2 material/inspection-station variation)? CNC-02 shows the highest vibration means (2.116 then 1.825) vs all other CNCs at ~1.35-1.706, but we only have its 450-550 window. Comparing CNC-02 vibration before the first failure (job 1 failed at tick 324) establishes whether this elevation is new.

Whether CNC-05 — the last machine before inspection, which every job passes through immediately before its inspection result — shows abnormal axis following_error during the failed jobs (1, 2, 4) but not during the passed job 3. That pattern would indicate an intermittent CNC-05 fault; a flat normal trend would favor inspection-station or within-batch variation (H2) over a machine cause.

The evidence settled whether CNC-05 following_error is abnormal during failed jobs 1, 2, and 4, and normal during passed job 3. It is not: the following_error is consistently elevated across all jobs, which contradicts H4 and supports H2. No further checks are needed to distinguish these hypotheses.

conclusion.diagnosis: Inspection failures (jobs 1, 2, 4) all occur immediately after CNC-05 processing, but no CNC fault is confirmed. CNC-02 vibration is elevated (means ~1.8-2.4) yet that elevation predates every failure (E18: ticks 60-450), so it is a long-standing baseline, not a new fault (H2b). All five CNCs show comparable recent vibration (E7, E11, E15-E17); CNC-05 vibration is normal (E7). CNC-05 following_error (E19) does not cleanly separate the passed job from the failed jobs: approximate window means are ~3.1 (job 1), ~3.7 (job 2), ~2.7 (job 3, passed), ~2.8 (job 4), and job 3's bucket maximum (4.483, ticks 390-419) even exceeds job 4's (4.15, ticks 480-509). So an intermittent CNC-05 fault (H4) is not supported by the signal data, while a CNC-04 fault (H1) is contradicted by clean CNC-04 vibration (E15). Cause remains isolated to neither a machine nor confirmed: inspection-station or incoming-material variation (H2) is possible but unverified, and no intervention reaches the 0.90 confidence threshold.

RUN-01.name: evidence_quality
RUN-01.instructions: Read `trace`. Judge whether the final `conclusion.diagnosis` is supported by relevant evidence the factory itself returned (origin 'observable'), rather than by assumptions, manual guidance or memory alone. Consider only evidence ids the conclusion or the selected hypothesis cites and what those items actually contain.
criteria: 0: The conclusion cites no observable evidence, or the cited evidence does not bear on the claim.
1: One cited observable item loosely relates to the claim; key symptoms the claim depends on were never read.
2: Cited observable evidence shows the symptom the claim names, but a plausible alternative explanation of the same evidence was not examined.
3: Cited observable evidence shows the symptom and at least one discriminating reading was made that separates the claim from an alternative.
4: Cited observable evidence shows the symptom, discriminating readings separate it from the alternatives, and other machines or batches were checked before the conclusion.
RUN-01.missing_evidence: If trace.completeness is record_only, do not ask; record unknown.
RUN-01.deterministic_precedence: evaluator_only.evidence_share and relevant_evidence_collected give the truth-side view of coverage; this question gives the judge's view of whether what was collected supports what was concluded. Report both, never one for the other.
RUN-01.scoring_note: Report the probability-weighted score and the modal level; a mean below 2 on a run scored root_cause_correct=true is flagged 'misleading success'.

RUN-02.name: hypothesis_reasoning
RUN-02.instructions: Read `trace.hypotheses`, `trace.pruned_candidates` and the decisions in phase 'test'. Judge whether the investigator considered competing plausible causes for the anomaly and tested them against each other, rather than pursuing one explanation from the start.
criteria: 0: One hypothesis only, or several hypotheses that are rewordings of the same cause.
1: Several distinct hypotheses were listed but no decision in the test phase was aimed at telling them apart.
2: Distinct hypotheses and at least one test-phase reading that bears on a rival, but confidences moved without the cited evidence changing.
3: Distinct hypotheses, discriminating readings, and confidences revised in a way the cited evidence explains.
4: As 3, and a hypothesis that needs no change to the factory (a transient, a batch, a setting) was held and tested, not only mechanical faults.

RUN-03.name: critic_effectiveness
RUN-03.instructions: Read `trace.critique`, `trace.recheck`, the hypotheses and the conclusion. Did the critic identify an important weakness (a contradiction, a missing check, a better alternative) and did a useful follow-up happen when one was warranted?

criteria.effective: The critic named a real weakness or the best-supported alternative, and the follow-up reading (or the conclusion) reflects it.
criteria.ineffective: The critic missed an evident weakness, objected without substance, or its point was available and ignored (recheck skipped, policy_stopped, or the conclusion unchanged despite a contradicting reading).
criteria.not_required: The leading hypothesis was already well supported and the critic's agreement was reasonable; no follow-up was needed.
criteria.unknown: No usable critique (outcome no_answer or invalid_reply), or the trace is incomplete.

RUN-03.missing_evidence: No critique record: not asked; recorded as not_run.
RUN-03.applies_to: one master-run packet with trace.critique present
RUN-03.deterministic_precedence: critique.verdict_mismatch, recheck.outcome and recheck.trigger are code facts; evaluator_only.critic_pick_correct says whether the pick named the true cause. Those are reported beside this answer.

RUN-04.name: retrieval_quality
RUN-04.instructions: Read `trace.manual_searches`, `trace.recall_searches`, the evidence items whose origin is 'manual' or 'memory', and where those ids are cited. Did the retrieved passages or memories materially support the investigation?

criteria.useful: A retrieved section or memory is cited by a hypothesis, a decision or the conclusion, and the reasoning that cites it is consistent with its content.
criteria.unnecessary: Retrieval happened but nothing retrieved was cited or acted on; the investigation would read the same without it.
criteria.misleading: A retrieved item was cited in support of a claim it does not support, or steered a reading away from the symptom.
criteria.not_retrieved: The tool was offered but never answered a search (no search, or every search refused or failed).

RUN-04.missing_evidence: Neither offered: not asked; recorded as not_offered.
RUN-04.applies_to: one master-run packet with manual or memory offered
RUN-04.deterministic_precedence: search counts, refusals and the sections returned are code facts (manual_searches, recall_searches); whether a memory was cited is `memory_uses.used` in the record.

RUN-05.name: verification_demonstrated
RUN-05.instructions: Read `trace.verification`, `trace.proposal` and the evidence observed after `action_finish_tick` (or after the conclusion for a no-action run). Does the trace show that the agent checked its prediction against observations made after the work, and that the verdict follows from them?

criteria.yes: Observable evidence with a data window after the work (or after the conclusion) was read, the verdict cites it, and the cited values agree with the verdict.
criteria.no: No look after the work, the verdict cites evidence from before the work, or the cited values contradict the verdict.
criteria.not_applicable: The run ended with escalate or without a proposal, so no remedy was there to verify.

RUN-05.deterministic_precedence: The loop already refuses a verdict that rests on evidence from before the work (`capstone.agent.investigation.verify`); evaluator_only.verification_calibration compares the verdict with the truth. This question adds only whether the cited numbers support the verdict.

RUN-06.name: abstention_appropriate
RUN-06.instructions: Read the conclusion, its confidence and assessment, and the evidence. If the agent declined to name a cause (escalate / unresolved) was the evidence in fact insufficient? If it named a cause with high confidence, was the evidence sufficient for that confidence?

criteria.appropriate: Declined when the evidence left two or more causes open, or committed when the cited evidence settles the cause.
criteria.inappropriate: Declined although the cited evidence settled the cause, or committed with confidence 0.8 or more while a rival cause was untested or a contradiction stood.
criteria.not_applicable: The run never reached a reasoned conclusion (model unavailable, undetermined by timeout).

RUN-06.deterministic_precedence: evaluator_only.abstained and confident_wrong are code facts from the label and the truth; this question judges the decision against the evidence shown, not against the truth.

RUN-07.name: failure_classification
RUN-07.instructions: Read the whole trace. What most seriously undermined this investigation? Choose the single earliest cause that, had it gone right, would most likely have changed the outcome.

criteria.reasoning: The relevant readings were in hand and misread: the hypotheses or confidences do not follow from the cited evidence.
criteria.retrieval: A manual or memory answer was absent, unhelpful or misleading at the point it mattered.
criteria.critic: The critic missed or misdirected, or its correct point was dropped.
criteria.tooling: Tool errors, refused calls, repeated calls, a blackout or a gap left the needed reading unavailable, or the budget ran out before it could be made.
criteria.verification: The diagnosis and action were right but the post-action check was missing or wrong.
criteria.none_observed: Nothing undermined it: the investigation reads as sound.

RUN-07.missing_evidence: record_only packets: the judge may use tools_used, decisions outcomes and termination_reason only; answer unknown unless a tooling or timeout cause is evident from them.
RUN-07.applies_to: one master-run packet; asked of every run, with none_observed for one that reads as sound, so the judge never learns from the question which runs were wrong
RUN-07.deterministic_precedence: evaluator_only.miss_kind (evidence_miss vs reasoning_miss) and facts.termination_reason are code facts reported beside this answer.

RUN-08.name: conclusion_support
RUN-08.instructions: Independently of whether the diagnosis is true, how well does the trace support the final conclusion as stated? Consider the cited evidence, the unexplained and contradicting evidence the hypotheses list, open questions, and whether the stated confidence matches.
criteria: 0: The conclusion is not supported: cited evidence is absent, irrelevant or contradicts it.
1: Weakly supported: one consistent reading, with alternatives or contradictions left open.
2: Partly supported: the symptom is shown, but at least one listed contradiction, unexplained item or open question remains.
3: Well supported: the cited evidence shows the symptom and separates the cause from the alternatives the agent considered.
4: Fully supported: as 3, with the confidence stated proportionate and nothing material left open.
RUN-08.deterministic_precedence: `check_conclusion` already lowers an unresolved conclusion to escalate; this question measures the quality of the text and citations, which code cannot.

RUN-11.name: critic_feedback_used
RUN-11.instructions: Read `trace.critique` (the check it named), `trace.recheck` and the hypotheses before and after. Did the investigator use the critic's feedback?

criteria.used: The follow-up reading was made where the critic pointed, and the leading hypothesis or its confidence changed in the direction the reading supports (or stayed when the reading confirmed it).
criteria.ignored: A usable critique named a check and the follow-up was skipped, stopped by the policy, refused, or made but the beliefs did not respond to what it showed.
criteria.no_feedback: The critic gave no usable check (no_answer, invalid_reply, or an empty discriminating_check).

RUN-11.missing_evidence: No recheck record: not asked (the follow-up was off).
RUN-11.applies_to: one master-run packet with trace.critique and trace.recheck present
RUN-11.deterministic_precedence: recheck.outcome, confidence_before and confidence_after are code facts; this question adds whether the response to the reading was sensible.

RUN-12.name: evidence_cited_matches_content
RUN-12.instructions: For each evidence id the conclusion cites, read that item's content. Does every cited item actually show what the conclusion says it shows?

criteria.true: Every cited item contains the reading, event or result the conclusion attributes to it.
criteria.false: At least one cited item does not contain what is attributed to it (wrong machine, wrong sensor, a value not present, an event not there), or the conclusion cites nothing.

RUN-12.deterministic_precedence: `check_conclusion` verifies that cited ids exist and `verify_numeric_claims` checks structured numbers; neither checks the prose. This question covers the prose.
